newsitem.title: GERMANY: Poll sees rising German fears about EMU.
newsitem.headline: Poll sees rising German fears about EMU.

text.p: German fears about giving up the mark for a single European currency are rising and many Germans are glum about their economic prospects once the euro is launched, an opinion poll published on Wednesday said.
Stern magazine said 61 percent of Germans polled now looked with fear to the planned economic and monetary union (EMU) while only 16 percent were hopeful about the euro currency.
The level of fear about the new currency rose from 53 percent in October 1995 and 57 percent in April of this year, according to the survey by the Allensbach polling organisation.
Only 26.4 percent of the 1,235 Germans polled in mid-November supported EMU while 47.4 percent opposed it, the survey showed. Another 26.2 percent were undecided.
Expectations about Germany's economic performance with the new currency were also glum, with 45.9 percent expecting higher inflation and 35.2 percent sure that unemployment would go up.

Those polled were also sceptical about EMU starting on time -- 46.3 percent thought it would not be launched in 1999. Of those sceptics, 77.9 percent expected EMU to come later rather than be scrapped altogether.
Allensbach said voters saw Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Europe's main champion of the single currency, and his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) as the best choice to lead Germany into the currency union.
Kohl's European policies were supported by 30.5 percent of the sample, got an "undecided" response from 30.8 percent and were opposed by 38.7 percent, the survey said.
But Oskar Lafontaine, head of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), won only 14.3 percent support for his European policies while 47.8 percent had no opinion and 37.8 percent opposed him.
Among the parties, the survey showed that 38.9 percent rated the CDU as the best party on European policy, compared to 46.8 percent who were undecided and only 11.7 percent who favoured the SPD.

The survey also showed that 42.5 percent of those polled thought Kohl made too many concessions to other members of the European Union, 27.5 thought his European policy was just right and 4.6 percent thought he should stand up more for Germany's interests in Brussels.
